title: How to choose between brokered CDs and bank CDs
description: Understanding liquidity, yield, and call risk in the fixed-income market.
content:
A Certificate of Deposit (CD) seems simple: lock money, get interest. But there are two very different ways to buy them. You can buy a **Bank CD** directly from a bank (like Ally or Chase), or you can buy a **Brokered CD** inside your investment account (like Fidelity or Vanguard). While they are both FDIC insured, they behave differently. Brokered CDs often pay higher rates and can be sold early on a secondary market, but they carry 'Call Risk' and price fluctuation risk if rates rise. This guide explains which one fits your portfolio.

Key Takeaways

  • Liquidity: Bank CDs charge a penalty (e.g., 3 months interest) to break early. Brokered CDs must be sold on the market; you might get back less than you put in if rates have risen.
  • Yield: Brokered CDs often yield 0.10% - 0.30% more because brokerages buy them in bulk blocks from banks.
  • Call Risk: Many Brokered CDs are 'Callable,' meaning the bank can cancel them if rates drop. Bank CDs are almost never callable.
  • Convenience: Brokered CDs allow you to hold CDs from 10 different banks in one Fidelity account, maximizing FDIC coverage to $2.5M+.

Why It Matters (US Context)

In a falling rate environment (like projected 2025/2026), 'Call Protection' is valuable. Banks want to cancel your high-rate CD if they can borrow cheaper elsewhere. Understanding the 'Non-Callable' filter is crucial for Brokered CD buyers.

Head-to-Head Comparison

Where should you buy your safety?

1. Bank CD (Direct)

  • Bought at: Ally.com, Marcus.com, Local Branch.
  • Early Exit: Fixed Penalty (e.g., 60 days interest). Principal is protected.
  • Interest: Compounds inside the CD (usually).
  • Best For: Emergency Funds, simple savers who want guaranteed principal protection even if they break it early.

2. Brokered CD (Secondary)

  • Bought at: Fidelity, Schwab, Vanguard.
  • Early Exit: Sell at market price. If rates rose, you sell at a loss (e.g., get $950 for a $1,000 CD). Principal NOT protected if sold early.
  • Interest: Paid out to your brokerage cash account (does not compound inside).
  • Best For: Retirees needing income, Ladder builders, high net worth (FDIC spreading).

The Selection Algorithm

  1. Check the 'Call' Attribute: When buying a Brokered CD, ensure it says 'Call Protection: YES' or 'Non-Callable'. If you buy a Callable CD at 5% and rates drop to 3%, the bank will call it away, and you lose your high yield.
  2. Compare Yields: Log into Fidelity. Check 1-year CD rates. Open a new tab for Ally. Compare. Often Fidelity wins.
  3. Assess Liquidity Needs: If there is a 10% chance you need this money for an emergency, buy the Bank CD. The penalty is predictable. Selling a Brokered CD in a panic can result in capital loss.
  4. Laddering: Brokered CDs are easier for laddering because you can see all maturities in one dashboard.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are they both FDIC insured?

Yes. Even Brokered CDs are issued by underlying banks and carry FDIC protection up to $250k per issuer. Fidelity just acts as the middleman.

Why doesn't interest compound in Brokered CDs?

They act like bonds. They pay 'coupons' into your core cash position. You have to manually use that cash to buy more CDs or stocks to get the compounding effect.

Can I transfer a CD?

Brokered CDs can be transferred between brokerages (ACATS). Bank CDs usually have to be cashed out to move.
